title: Layer 4 Spiny Stellate Cells
intro: Layer 4 is the cortex's main entrance for sensory input from the thalamus, and in primary sensory areas many of its excitatory cells are spiny stellate cells: star-shaped, spiny neurons without a long apical dendrite, whose axons stay inside the local column. They amplify the thalamic signal and pass it up to layer 2/3.

items: Morphology: a round soma with several spiny dendrites radiating in all directions and no prominent apical dendrite. In rodent barrel cortex the dendrites of spiny stellates point into their own barrel, so each cell samples input from one whisker (Feldmeyer et al. 1999).

Where they are: layer 4 of primary sensory areas, notably rodent somatosensory (barrel) cortex and primate V1 layer 4C. Other areas and species use small 'star pyramids' or ordinary pyramidal cells in layer 4, and motor cortex has little or no layer 4.

Inputs: core (first-order) thalamic axons from the ventral posterior medial nucleus (barrels) or the lateral geniculate nucleus (V1), and, in much larger numbers, other layer 4 cells. Thalamic synapses are only roughly 5 to 20 per cent of the excitatory synapses on a layer 4 cell, but they are strong and synchronous (Benshalom & White 1986; Bruno & Sakmann 2006).

Outputs: local only. Axons target layer 4 and especially layer 2/3 within the same column, a strong and reliable projection (Feldmeyer et al. 2002). They are intratelencephalic but essentially never leave the area.
Firing: regular spiking with adaptation; some bursting cells in layer 4 are reported.

Recurrent amplification: layer 4 excitatory cells connect to one another fairly densely (connection probability around 0.2 to 0.3 within a barrel), amplifying the thalamic input (Douglas et al. 1995 argued this recurrent gain is a basic cortical operation).

blocks.text: The same thalamic axons that drive layer 4 excitatory cells also drive PV interneurons, even more strongly, and those PV cells inhibit the excitatory cells about a millisecond later (Gabernet et al. 2005; Cruikshank et al. 2007). This feedforward inhibition gives layer 4 cells a very short window, a few milliseconds, in which coincident thalamic spikes can make them fire. Layer 4 cells are therefore coincidence detectors for synchronous thalamic input. In cat V1 this mechanism, together with the alignment of thalamic inputs (Hubel & Wiesel 1962), helps create orientation-selective simple cells.

items: Detailed: Blue Brain's L4_SS (spiny stellate), L4_SP (star pyramid) and L4_PC m-types with fitted e-types (Markram et al. 2015). Lefort et al. (2009) and Feldmeyer's paired recordings give the connection probabilities and amplitudes used to wire them.
Point neurons: LIF, Izhikevich regular spiking or AdEx. Because spiny stellates have compact dendrites, a point neuron is a better approximation for them than for pyramidal cells.

Circuit models of layer 4: the Troyer et al. (1998) and McLaughlin et al. (2000) V1 layer 4 models explain orientation tuning from thalamic input plus cortical inhibition; Sarid et al. (2007) modelled a barrel's layer 4 to layer 2/3 module with reconstructed cells; Potjans-Diesmann layer 4 is an LIF population of about 21,900 excitatory cells.
In HTM and the Thousand Brains Theory, layer 4 is the 'input layer' that represents sensory features at locations, with location signals arriving from layer 6 (Lewis et al. 2019).

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: Model layer 4 excitatory cells as point neurons with local-only output to layer 2/3 and layer 4.
Drive them with a sparse, strong, synchronous input population (the thalamus) and pair it with feedforward PV inhibition; without it, layer 4 loses timing precision.
Use recurrent layer 4 connections modestly: they amplify, but too much gain turns layer 4 into a runaway excitatory loop.
If you follow the Thousand Brains model, layer 4 cells also need a modulatory location input (a distal dendritic segment in HTM terms) from layer 6.
